question: Why shouldn’t that worry me?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt leads in practice.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. He makes intent explicit, pushes decisions to the people closest to the work, and coaches teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks. Across roles that included leading a **150-person** Cloud Innovation Center at **Accenture**, he inherited engineering teams that were “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.”

He built balanced teams with engineers, product managers, and UX architects sharing accountability. Instead of relying on hierarchical handoffs, he embedded pair programming, collaborative coding, retrospectives, and open feedback. Teams could voice concerns and implement changes autonomously. His leadership philosophy story reports **4x delivery acceleration** once teams embraced lean product and modern engineering practices. His balanced-team work reports **zero-defect production code** across client engagements.

His “permit to fail” environment included non-punitive post-mortems and lean, low-stakes experiments. Teams that had avoided risks because of fear of blame began testing new approaches and applying lessons to subsequent sprints. In product incubation, he set expectations that prototypes and user tests would likely fail intentionally, then used user research and rapid testing to validate assumptions before committing to costly builds.

At **Norfolk Southern**, rising defects exposed a problem that near-complete test coverage had hidden. Matt took ownership in front of the client and **Accenture** account leadership rather than defending the metrics. He audited the code and tests, showed the gaps openly, and rebuilt vague backlog stories with defined scenarios and a definition of done.

He brought in TDD experts to work alongside engineers and used boot camps, coding katas, and an “I do, we do, you do” coaching progression. Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Yes. At **Norfolk Southern**, the working practices Matt introduced did not hold at first.

Matt launched the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement in early **2020**, modernizing the client’s legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. He brought in a balanced team and emphasized test-driven development. A couple of months later, as the pandemic moved everyone to remote work, the client reported rising defects. The dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The failure landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

An engineer had been building from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete while defects went undetected. The backlog also contained vague stories without defined scenarios or a definition of done. Pairing, test-first development, and continuous integration had been introduced, but the reinforcement and verification had been missing.

Matt took ownership rather than defending the metrics. He audited the codebase and test suite, showed the gaps openly, and rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories. He brought in frontend and backend TDD experts to work alongside engineers and redo the code and tests properly.

He then changed the daily workflow: test cases came before the solution, inside rotating pairs, with progress checked at standup. New engineers paired with seasoned practitioners. Instead of relying on a mandate or dashboard, the team practiced through coding katas and an “I do, we do, you do” progression.

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. After the experts left, pairing and test-first remained the team’s default, and the failure mode did not recur.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a **Fortune 500 financial services client**, with dev, QA, UAT, and production environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead, he relied on that documentation without confirming its accuracy. He focused on delivery pressures rather than validating access patterns, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not implement compensating controls such as data masking or email interception. He also did not verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**. The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described it as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work, from payment engines and global gateways to developer integration.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, treasury services ran on multiple regional and legacy payment systems with different data models, entitlements, and compliance records. The new ACCESS platform used Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries foundation, but the bank needed payment capabilities beyond its out-of-box offering for **135,000+** clients across **180+** countries.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and bank resources in the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and government tax payment modules. That included NACHA file validation, payment-type-specific entitlements, Message Authentication Code security, sanctions screening, and contextual help explaining payment fields and requirements.

He also designed the centralized payments gateway, handling message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12** countries. Corporate treasurers gained a single entry point for Wire, ACH, and Cross-Border Transfers instead of separate local logins and regional systems. Matt led the payments data migration, preserving client configurations, transaction histories, and compliance traceability **without disruption to live payment operations**. ACCESS launched in April **2011**. He also owned on-call and production incident response.

At **American Express**, Matt’s work addressed a different payments problem: clients struggled to adopt the Virtual Payments Platform because SDKs were missing, documentation was fragmented, and there was no sandbox. Dependency bottlenecks also delayed developers’ testing.

Matt co-created the developer portal, developed Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, and introduced use case-driven documentation, sample integrations, and a secure sandbox. He coordinated virtualized testing environments, used Lean Product and XP practices, and conducted a Client Onboarding Test Drive to gather user feedback.

Client onboarding time decreased, and API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch. The portal team also exceeded its delivery commitment by over **261 story points** of customer-focused value.

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt built and ran the organization.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Centers in Atlanta and Tampa, Matt scaled an initial **10-person** pilot to **150+ practitioners** over **4 years**. The stories describe that starting point, rather than **4 people**, and the organization included engineering, architecture, product, and design. Many new hires lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience, so expansion required recruiting, practical training, and a management model that worked without adding layers of supervisors.

Matt built a hiring engine across internal bench searches, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and approved job requisitions. Engineers completed hands-on TDD pairing auditions, while product managers and designers worked through live scoping exercises. Interviewers recorded independent votes, and Matt held the closing interview and made every final hiring decision. During scaling pushes, the process produced **4 to 6 net-new practitioners per week**. Interview participation was capped at **2 slots per practitioner per week** to protect delivery time.

New joiners moved through structured enablement, then round-robin pairing with experienced practitioners. The learning model was “I do, we do, you do,” progressing from guided work to independent delivery. Matt embedded pair programming, TDD, CI/CD, user-centered design, peer-led tech talks, and retrospectives into daily work rather than treating training as a separate activity.

The organization stayed deliberately flat, with **11 to 13 practice and client leads** reporting directly to Matt. Team anchors kept leads informed without another management layer. Monday allocation reviews matched people to engagements and learning assignments. Because managers did not sit on daily teams, performance reviews drew on evidence from recent pair partners, product managers, and anchors. Matt also ran promotion calibration, compensation allocation, and remediation decisions.

The organization reached **150+ practitioners**, with near-zero attrition during its first **2 years**. Across CIC delivery, **10-person** balanced teams delivered output equivalent to traditional **20-person** teams, with **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS Next Generation needed capabilities beyond Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform. The bank served **135,**000+ clients** across 180+ countries**, with distinct payment formatting, validation, compliance, and workflow requirements. Regional systems also had different data models, entitlements, and transaction histories that had to move without interrupting live payments.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a **40+ person** blended team across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules. The work included NACHA file validation, Message Authentication Code security, payment-type-specific permissions, sanctions screening, and integration with centralized transaction monitoring. He also owned on-call and production incident response.

Matt designed the centralized payments gateway for connectivity across **12 countries**, handling message transformation, protocol translation, and routing to clearing networks and internal settlement systems. For the legacy migration, he coordinated data verification with compliance teams, introduced compliance dashboards, and ran production validation and post-cutover defect triage. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**; the migration completed **without disruption to live payment operations**, preserving compliance traceability.

At **RBC**, fragmented systems and manual processes were delaying cross-border and bulk payments. Matt designed workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation, including real-time FX integration, automated alerts, recurring payments, Interac e-Transfer, and batch processing. He delivered an implementation blueprint, and revised payment cutoff processes reduced wire-transfer delays.

At **American Express**, adoption of its Virtual Payments Platform lagged because clients lacked SDKs, consistent documentation, and a sandbox. Matt co-created a developer portal, developed Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, and built a secure sandbox with refreshed client data. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, client onboarding time decreased, and adoption accelerated migration away from legacy systems.

🐾 Found it! Matt was brought in roughly seven months into **Fiserv**'s 14-month, **$8.5M** white-label card portal program, the shared platform behind branded credit card sites for **2M+** cardholders across **15** financial institutions. The **45-person** globally dispersed team had missed multiple consecutive deadlines, and client stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation. He recovered a Q4 release that was **3 weeks** behind, avoiding **$500K** in penalties, and the program was delivered **3%** under budget with zero critical defects at launch.

Want to hear how he moved that team from 6-month waterfall releases to 2-week sprints?

🐾 Here’s how Matt changed the working model.

At **Fiserv**, the **45-person** team was working through **6-month** waterfall release cycles, with requirements buried in **200-page** business requirements documents organized by system modules. Developers in India, testers in the Philippines, and designers in Ireland had no visibility into work status. Deadlines kept slipping, stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation, and PMO and compliance teams resisted agile.

Matt changed how work was defined and tracked, rather than just adding sprint meetings. He decomposed the requirements into persona-based user stories and replaced a single To Do/Done JIRA board with a multi-tiered Kanban/Scrum architecture. The **47** acceptance criteria became Epics, with user stories moving through specific workflow columns.

He established follow-the-sun synchronization: **7 AM CST** scrum-of-scrums for offshore-to-onshore handoffs and **11 PM CST** syncs for the reverse handoff. Bi-weekly demos gave **Fiserv** stakeholders early opportunities to sign off on branding, UI, and ADA compliance instead of discovering problems at month **6**. When reviewers lacked bandwidth, he negotiated dedicated review windows.

For compliance, Matt retained steering committee reporting while adding sprint-level visibility. He used JIRA as the system of record, with audit trails, attached ADA scans, and developer comments instead of static Word documents. He coached offshore teams on empowerment over command-and-control and built JAWS/NVDA screen reader audits into the Definition of Done. Alongside that work, mandatory code reviews, unit tests, and automated build quality gates addressed the portal’s production quality problems.

The team moved to **2-week** sprints within **3 months**. JIRA provided real-time visibility to **50+** stakeholders across **3** time zones, and PMO and compliance accepted it as the system of record. The recovered program met all **47** acceptance criteria with zero critical defects at launch.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s the story behind Matt’s **Norfolk Southern** work.

As a Director at **Accenture**, Matt led the Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement: modernizing **Norfolk Southern’s** Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. Its mainframe dated to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce, and clerks manually handled waybill and rating fallout. Wholesale replacement was too risky: modernization had to happen without stopping the railroad. The client was accustomed to mainframe thinking, account leadership to waterfall delivery, and his team was learning a new working model during the pandemic.

Matt started with domain-driven design and event storming to map embedded business functions and dependencies. He used the Boris Exercise to map APIs and data flows, and SNAP-E documentation to capture dependencies and risks. Rather than a big-bang cutover, he built APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB alongside the mainframe, using change data capture and reconciliation to validate that nothing was lost. API gateways, anti-corruption layers, Docker, Kubernetes, and automated CI/CD supported incremental replacement.

When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought its revenue management team into the innovation hub to co-create. They developed the Shipper Revenue System interface through personas, user flows, and prototypes in weekly build-measure-learn iterations. The MVP launched covering **95%** of targeted use cases, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. EDI validation caught fallout at the front door and notified trading partners instead of waiting for customer complaints.

The engagement also encountered rising defects despite near-complete test coverage. Matt audited the code and tests, found tests written after code and vague backlog stories, and brought in TDD experts for hands-on coaching. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

For enablement, he led a **two-day** CIC Academy course **twice a month** over **6 months**. Pairing rotated scarce legacy knowledge through the team, while client contributors learned Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native concepts. They learned to own their backlog and priorities and support the application after **Accenture** rolled off.

He also published and presented a client-specific migration strategy to senior leadership; **RBC** adopted it.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s the story behind Matt’s **RBC** work.

As Senior Technology Architecture Manager, Matt worked on the Day**2Day** Corporate Banking modernization, evaluating Bottomline WebSeries as the payment hub engine to replace **RBC** Express. The existing systems struggled with performance and scalability and lacked digital offerings. Leadership needed to know whether the proposed platform could meet business requirements before committing further investment.

Matt conducted an architecture assessment and gap/fit analysis across Data, Application, Technology, and Business Architecture. He reviewed code, interviewed stakeholders, analyzed documentation, and created architectural heat maps. Working with the enterprise architecture team, he developed logical and system models with a transparent cost-to-fix versus benefit comparison. The assessment found that WebSeries lacked the modularity required for **RBC**’s long-term digital operating model. That finding prevented investment in a platform path that could not deliver and enabled the bank to redirect technical resources toward higher-priority initiatives.

Alongside that assessment, Matt established the PMO during discovery and requirements. He maintained the program roadmap and dependencies, consolidated financial, quality, resource, and project reporting, and introduced designated team contacts, real-time updates, daily summaries, and a task-tracking matrix. The governance framework coordinated **3 organizations**: **RBC**, **Accenture**, and Bottomline Technologies. It eliminated missed program updates and reduced redundant effort.

When the previous data conversion lead left, Matt took over that workstream from scratch. He analyzed decades-old payment records, documented source-to-target transformation rules, planned mock conversion cycles, and established reconciliation checks for payment amounts and beneficiary details. He also managed onshore and offshore teams performing data scrubbing and validation.

For mobile readiness, Matt defined API integration points, cheque deposit requirements, and cross-browser and cross-device scalability needs. He delivered a modernization blueprint; the architecture assessment’s heat maps and roadmap artifacts remained reference material for future planning.

question: How long did that take?

answer_md:
🐾 Tracking this down...

Matt led **Norfolk Southern’s** Revenue and Shipment Planning modernization as the **Accenture** Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement. Its mainframe dated to the **1970s**. Orders could fall out unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly, and clerks manually handled waybill and rating fallout. Wholesale replacement was too risky: modernization had to happen without stopping the railroad. The client was accustomed to mainframe thinking, account leadership to waterfall delivery, and Matt’s team was learning a new working model during the transition to remote work.

Matt led domain-driven design and event storming sessions to map business functions and dependencies. Rather than attempt a big-bang cutover, his team kept the mainframe as the system of record while building APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB alongside it. Change data capture synchronized the platforms; reconciliation checked that nothing was lost. API gateways, anti-corruption layers, asynchronous messaging, and SNAP-E documentation supported incremental replacement, with Docker, Kubernetes, and automated CI/CD carrying the new services.

When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought its revenue management team into the innovation hub to co-create. They developed the Shipper Revenue System interface from personas through high-fidelity prototypes in weekly build-measure-learn iterations. EDI validation caught malformed data at the front door rather than waiting for customer complaints.

The engagement also encountered rising defects despite near-complete test coverage. Matt took ownership, audited the code and tests, and found tests written after code alongside vague backlog stories. He brought in TDD experts, rebuilt testable stories, and introduced coding katas and hands-on coaching. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

Matt also led a **2-day** CIC Academy course, delivered twice monthly over **6 months**. Pairing used “I do, we do, you do” to share scarce legacy knowledge and teach Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native concepts.

The MVP launched covering **95%** of targeted use cases, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. The client team was co-creating in weekly iterations, and its contributors gained skills to support the new application after **Accenture** rolled off.
